variants.name: Explicit loop in the emitted JavaScript
variants.implementation_notes: At runtime TypeScript is JavaScript, so the realization is the loop: type the state parameters, then reassign them in a while/for loop with the base case as the guard. TypeScript adds nothing here - the compiler does not emit a trampoline and no target/emit setting changes tail-call behaviour - so a function that recurses in tail position grows the stack exactly as its JavaScript source would. The type system's own tail-recursion elimination (the sibling variant) is a different mechanism at a different level and does not help the runtime.
pitfalls: No target or emit downleveling introduces elimination, and neither does --alwaysStrict: the runtime behaviour is the engine's, not the compiler's.
A recursive generic function such as sumTo<N extends number>(...) reads as if it might be compiled away; it is an ordinary JavaScript function and still overflows.
Type-only recursion and value recursion are easy to conflate: a type that the checker eliminates proves nothing about the function with the same name.

variants.name: Type-level tail-recursion elimination on conditional types
variants.idiom_name: accumulator type parameter on a recursive conditional type
variants.implementation_notes: TypeScript 4.5 performs tail-recursion elimination on conditional types: when one branch of a conditional type is directly another conditional type, the checker avoids the intermediate instantiation that would otherwise trip the instantiation-depth heuristic. The technique mirrors the runtime pattern - move the partial result into an accumulator type parameter and make the recursive reference the returned branch, as TrimLeft and character-splitting types do - which keeps parsers and string routers working on inputs that previously produced 'Type instantiation is excessively deep'. This is a compile-time realization only; it says nothing about the stack at runtime.
pitfalls: Using the recursive result - Char | GetChars<Rest, Acc> - reintroduces intermediate instantiations and the excessively-deep error, exactly as consuming the value would break a runtime tail call.
The elimination is heuristic relief, not an infinite budget: extremely large inputs still hit limits, so a type-level parser needs its own size bound.
It is easy to mistake this for runtime support; any function with the same name still grows the stack when executed.
